issues.legal_issue: A person affected by an original decree, despite not being a party to the suit, may appeal from the decree with the court’s leave.
material_facts: The decree was passed by a High Court exercising original jurisdiction.
The applicants seeking recall were not parties to the suit but claimed to be affected by the decree concerning the property.
The applicants could have sought leave to appeal from the original decree.
issues.conclusion: An affected non-party may appeal from an original decree with the leave of the court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 provides for appeals from decrees passed in original jurisdiction. Although it does not specify who may appeal, an affected person who was not a party to the suit may appeal with the court’s leave; the person must be affected by the judgment and decree challenged.

predicates.appeal_from_original_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree passed by a court exercising original jurisdiction.
predicates.person_not_party_to_suit: The person seeking to appeal was not a party to the suit in which the decree was passed.
predicates.person_affected_by_decree: The decree affects the person seeking to appeal.

issues.definition: When a person outside a suit is affected by its original decree, that person may appeal if the court grants leave.

issues.legal_issue: The inherent power to recall a final decree cannot be used when an effective remedy for challenging the decree is available under the Code of Civil Procedure.
material_facts: The applicants were third parties to the suit and sought recall of a final decree by invoking the court’s inherent powers.
The decree was passed by the High Court exercising original jurisdiction and was therefore appealable.
The applicants could have sought leave to appeal as persons affected by the decree but instead pursued recall under the court’s inherent powers.
The recall application alleged that the decree had been obtained by fraud.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in using its inherent powers to recall the decree when an effective alternative remedy was available; its order allowing recall was set aside. The Court did not doubt that a court may recall an order obtained by fraud on the court, but held that the inherent power is restricted where another remedy is provided.
issues.legal_principle: Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 preserves inherent powers to meet the ends of justice or prevent abuse of process, but those powers cannot conflict with express procedure, override statutory restrictions, or substitute for an available remedy such as an appeal. Under Section 96, an affected non-party may appeal from an original decree with leave. The Court relied on Padam Sen v. State of U.P., AIR 1961 SC 218, which limits inherent powers where they conflict with the Code; Indian Bank v. Satyam Fibres (India) Pvt. Ltd., (1996) 5 SCC 550, which recognizes recall for fraud on the court while distinguishing fraud on a party; and Ram Prakash Agarwal v. Gopi Krishan, (2013) 11 SCC 296, which states that inherent powers are available only where no other remedy is provided and cannot be used in conflict with an existing remedy.

predicates.recall_application_under_inherent_power: A party asks a court to recall an order or decree by invoking the court’s inherent procedural power.
predicates.final_decree_under_challenge: The order sought to be recalled finally determines the proceeding or an issue in it.
predicates.effective_alternative_remedy_available: The party has an effective remedy under an existing legal procedure for challenging the order or decree.

issues.definition: A request to recall a final decree through inherent power is improper when an effective alternative procedure is available to challenge it.

issues.legal_issue: A judge’s prior representation of a party in a connected proceeding may make recusal appropriate to preserve the appearance of impartial justice, and an objection should be raised at the first opportunity.
material_facts: The senior judge had represented a party in a connected proceeding concerning the subject property while practising as an advocate.
The appellant did not raise that circumstance before the High Court or bring it to the judge’s attention at the first instance.
The Supreme Court expressed no doubt about the judge’s actual impartiality but considered that recusal would have been more appropriate in light of the appearance of possible bias.
issues.conclusion: Although the Court found no actual bias, it considered recusal more appropriate in the circumstances and observed that the appellant should have raised the issue at the first opportunity rather than belatedly.
issues.legal_principle: Justice must not only be done but must also be seen to be done. The Court applied the appearance-of-bias approach stated in State of West Bengal v. Shivananda Pathak, (1998) 5 SCC 513, relying on the principles in Metropolitan Properties Co. v. Lannon, (1968) 1 WLR 815, and Manak Lal v. Dr. Prem Chand Singhvi, AIR 1957 SC 425, and referred to R v. Sussex Justices, ex parte McCarthy, 1924 (1) KB 256. The relevant question is whether right-minded persons would consider there to be a real likelihood of bias; the objection should be raised promptly.

predicates.judicial_hearing: A judge is hearing and deciding a contentious judicial proceeding.
predicates.judge_previously_represented_party_in_co: Before becoming a judge, the judge represented a party in a proceeding connected to the matter being heard.
predicates.appearance_of_real_likelihood_of_bias: The circumstances could lead right-minded observers to perceive a real likelihood of bias, even if actual bias is absent.

issues.definition: In a judicial hearing, recusal is appropriate when a judge’s prior representation in a connected proceeding creates an apparent real likelihood of bias.
